subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If the distance from 'P' to the points (2,3) and (2,−3) are in the ratio 2:3, then find the equation of locus of P.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say what you would do with the ratio first, and name the shape the locus turns out to be.

steps.label: Take the locus point
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own. A ratio question, not a sum — and a ratio is far easier, because it squares away in one move.
lines: Let P = (x, y) be a point on the locus.

recall.must_convey: That the moving point is named P = (x, y) and the fixed points are written down.
accept: let P be x comma y
take the locus point as P x y
P equals x comma y is on the locus
locus point ni P x y ga teesukovali
name the moving point P with coordinates x and y

steps.why: Every locus question starts the same way: the moving point gets coordinates, and the condition is then written in terms of those coordinates.
common_mistakes: Giving the moving point fixed numbers instead of (x, y).
Mixing up which points are fixed and which one moves.

steps.label: Write the given condition
steps.margin_note: First mark, printed in the book's margin. Cross-multiply the ratio, then square BOTH sides at once — a ratio has no cross term, so one squaring clears both roots.

recall.must_convey: That the ratio is cross-multiplied to 3PA = 2PB and squared to 9PA² = 4PB².
accept: cross multiply to get three P A equals two P B then square to nine P A squared equals four P B squared
P A by P B is two by three so three P A is two P B
square both sides to get nine P A square equals four P B square
ratio ni cross multiply chesi square cheyyali
nine times P A squared equals four times P B squared

steps.why: A ratio of distances squares cleanly in one step, unlike a sum — there is no cross term to worry about, which is why this family is shorter than the ellipse family.
common_mistakes: Squaring to 3PA² = 2PB² and forgetting to square the numbers too.

steps.label: Substitute the distances
steps.margin_note: Second mark, also printed. Both distances go in squared. Note the two brackets differ only in the sign inside the y-term, because A and B differ only in the sign of their y-coordinate.

recall.must_convey: That both squared distances are written in coordinates, with 9 multiplying the A bracket and 4 the B bracket.
accept: substitute the distance formula into both sides keeping the nine and the four outside
put x minus two whole squared plus y minus three whole squared on the left
expand both brackets in coordinates
distance formula substitute chesi rendu brackets expand cheyyali
nine into the A bracket and four into the B bracket

steps.why: The two brackets are near-twins, differing only where the fixed points differ, so most of the expansion is the same work done twice.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the bracket contents by 9 and 4 unevenly.
Sign slip on (y + 3)², which expands with +6y.

steps.label: Simplify to the locus
steps.margin_note: The last two marks, printed as '2 Marks'. The x² and y² coefficients survive EQUAL (both 5), so this locus is a circle — the circle of Apollonius for the ratio 2:3.

recall.must_convey: That collecting terms gives the circle 5x² + 5y² − 20x − 78y + 65 = 0.
accept: collect all the terms to get five x squared plus five y squared minus twenty x minus seventy eight y plus sixty five equals zero
the x squared and y squared coefficients are both five so it is a circle
bring everything to one side and simplify
anni terms okavaipuku teesukoni simplify chesthe circle vasthundi
the locus is a circle

steps.why: When two distances are in a fixed ratio that is not 1:1, the locus is always a circle — the circle of Apollonius. Equal x² and y² coefficients confirm the algebra landed right.
